forces: Mixed chorus, baritone solo, orchestra and organ
performers: Bernard Kruysen, baritone; Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: Bernard Kruysen sings over a steady pizzicato in the cellos and basses. This movement contains the Requiem’s brief passage on judgement, with faster music, brass and the choir singing “Dies irae”.

sections.label: C · Horns announce the day of wrath
A′ · Plucked strings return to the opening pulse
sections.mNote: The opening rhythm returns beneath the choir’s luceat eis.

sections.label: A″ · Baritone melody in choral unison
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns, sung by the choir in unison.

sections.label: Coda · Baritone solo, then choir pp
sections.mNote: A last solo prayer, followed by the choir pianissimo.

cues.title: Baritone solo over pizzicato ostinato
cues.text: Cellos and basses play two pizzicato crotchets, rest, then pick up the next bar. Over this repeated pattern the baritone sings “Libera me, Domine” (deliver me, Lord) in a wide-ranging melody with sudden leaps.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 92–96: pizzicato ostinato and baritone solo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Libera me for baritone, 1877
cues.text: In 1877 Fauré wrote Libera me as a separate piece for baritone. In the same year he became choirmaster at the Madeleine. The first Requiem was heard there eleven years later, and the earlier music was added to it in later revisions.
cues.evidence: Composition and revision history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9). Madeleine appointment: https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/composer/gabriel-faure/biography

cues.title: Choral entry, “Tremens factus sum ego”
cues.text: The choir sings “Tremens factus sum ego” (I am made to tremble), its four parts moving together, pianissimo. The lower strings change from pizzicato to arco, and the baritone rests.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 97–98, rehearsal C: pp choral entry and arco lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dies irae, Più mosso
cues.text: The marking changes to Più mosso, and the horns enter fortissimo. The choir sings “Dies illa, dies irae” in chords, and trombones join the brass. Fauré sets the words in six beats to the bar.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 99–102: Più mosso, 6/4, horn chords and the choral Dies irae with trombones.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dies irae text, Aubert’s sleeve note
cues.text: Fauré left out the long Dies irae sequence of the Requiem Mass, but its words appear in this movement. Louis Aubert, who sang in the Madeleine choir as a boy, wrote on this recording’s sleeve that it passes “as an indispensable episode”.
cues.evidence: Louis Aubert’s note on the Erato sleeve (Internet Archive scan): “Le Dies irae y passe comme un épisode indispensable”, translation ours. https://archive.org/details/faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux. Fauré set only the Pie Jesu section of the sequence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9) (Text).

cues.title: Requiem aeternam, rehearsal F
cues.text: After the day of wrath the choir sings “Requiem aeternam”, piano. The 6/4 metre continues, and the strings keep moving underneath.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 102–104, rehearsal F: Requiem aeternam marked p in the continuing 6/4 metre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Unison return of the baritone melody
cues.text: The opening melody returns in the whole choir, sung in unison by sopranos, altos, tenors and basses. Kruysen sang it alone at the start. The repeated bass pattern is back beneath it.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 105–109: return of Moderato and the unison reprise of the baritone melody on p. 107.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the baritone, Kruysen
cues.text: The baritone sings the opening words once more over quiet repeated chords, and the choir follows pianissimo. In the last bar the strings play arco again and hold a D minor chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 112–113: baritone return, choral answer and final arco chord with fermatas.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Baritone solo to choral “Tremens”
transitions.how: The baritone finishes and the plucked bass pattern stops. At C the cellos take up the bow beneath the choir’s pianissimo “Tremens”. The four choral parts move together above sustained lower strings, and the organ continues underneath.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 96–97: the end of the solo and the choir’s entry at C.

transitions.title: Horns enter at Più mosso in 6/4
transitions.to: C · Horns announce the day of wrath
transitions.how: The choir ends on “ventura ira” and stops. At Più mosso the metre changes from common time to 6/4, and the horns begin the next passage fortissimo. The choir enters with “Dies illa, dies irae”, and the trombones join with forceful chords in the strings.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 99–101: tempo and metre change, horns and subsequent trombone entry.

transitions.title: The choir drops to piano
transitions.from: C · Horns announce the day of wrath
transitions.how: The day-of-wrath chords make a diminuendo into “Requiem aeternam”, marked piano at rehearsal F. The six-beat metre continues. Violins and violas keep up a moving accompaniment above the low strings, and the brass play more softly as the choir does.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 102: diminuendo into rehearsal F and the piano prayer for rest.

transitions.title: The bass pattern returns first
transitions.to: A′ · Plucked strings return to the opening pulse
transitions.how: Moderato restores common time and the opening bass rhythm. The strings play pizzicato again, with timpani reinforcing the rhythm. Altos and basses are still finishing “luceat eis” when the bass rhythm returns, and the opening melody comes back only after this.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 105–106, rehearsal H: Moderato, common time, pizzicato strings and timpani.

transitions.title: One melody for the whole choir
transitions.from: A′ · Plucked strings return to the opening pulse
transitions.to: A″ · Baritone melody in choral unison
transitions.how: Above the restored bass pattern, the choir sings the baritone’s opening D minor melody in unison, marked piano dolce. The strings repeat their chords. Horns and trombones add quiet harmony, and the timpani play intermittently, with gaps between their notes.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 106–109: unison reprise, repeated strings and intermittent brass and timpani.

transitions.title: The baritone returns to D minor
transitions.from: A″ · Baritone melody in choral unison
transitions.to: Coda · Baritone solo, then choir pp
transitions.how: The choir makes a diminuendo, and the baritone returns alone on “Libera me” over repeated string and organ chords. The choir follows pianissimo. The music stays in D minor through the closing bars, and the strings bow the final chord under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 111–113: diminuendo, solo return, choral answer and final D minor chord.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: VI. Libera me, printed pp. 92–113: baritone and plucked low strings, choral Tremens, the brass-led Dies irae, timpani at the returning ostinato, and the final solo with choral answers.

timeline.note: Plucked cellos and basses repeat their short pattern under the baritone. The organ holds long notes.
Violins and violas enter with held chords above the plucked bass line.
The choir takes over from the baritone, singing “Tremens” pianissimo in four parts.
Fortissimo horns play the faster, six-beat Dies irae.
Trombones join the horns as the choir and strings take the Dies irae forward.
The choir sings “Requiem aeternam” piano and dolce. The horns and trombones also play more quietly.
Plucked strings and timpani bring back the opening rhythm under the choir’s last “luceat eis”.
Horns and trombones enter quietly with chords above the repeated bass pattern.
The whole choir sings the baritone’s opening melody in unison. Timpani punctuate it with occasional quiet notes.
The baritone returns over repeated pianissimo chords. The choir answers; bowed strings hold the final chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Bernard Kruysen (baritone), Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; Kruysen is the baritone soloist here (the sleeve credits “Bernard Kruysen, baryton”). Denis Thilliez has no part in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.44 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 2 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.49 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: Organist and teacher who wrote songs and chamber music in an unusual harmonic language.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
As a boy, Fauré often went into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and Gabriel Fauré’s first musical experiences were on the small instrument in its chapel. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he studied plainchant, the organ and the polyphony of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was over, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers well outside their syllabus. Saint-Saëns became Fauré’s teacher, champion and friend, and remained so for sixty years. Fauré left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine, a setting of a French prayer over a flowing keyboard part, in which each new choral entry joins a phrase already under way.
